sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Schema design mistakes are expensive — fixing them after deployment requires migrations, data transforms, and often downtime. Interviewers test normalization to see if you can spot data redundancy problems, and ACID to see if you understand why banks don't lose transactions. Freshers who can explain why an index speeds up queries — and what it costs — demonstrate an engineering mindset beyond just coding.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
- **1NF** = each cell has a single atomic value; no repeating groups or arrays in a column
- **2NF** = 1NF + no partial dependency (every non-key column depends on the WHOLE primary key, not just part of it — relevant for composite PKs)
- **3NF** = 2NF + no transitive dependency (non-key column A should not depend on non-key column B which depends on the PK)
- **PRIMARY KEY** = uniquely identifies each row; cannot be NULL; only one per table
- **FOREIGN KEY** = enforces referential integrity; references the PK of another table
- **INDEX** = data structure (usually B-tree) that speeds up reads by creating a sorted lookup; costs write overhead
- **ACID** = Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (constraints hold), Isolation (transactions don't interfere), Durability (committed data survives crashes)
- **Dirty read** = reading uncommitted data from another transaction
- **Non-repeatable read** = same query returns different data within same transaction
- **Phantom read** = same query returns different ROWS due to another transaction inserting/deleting

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- `normalization` — drill: 1NF (atomic), 2NF (no partial dependency), 3NF (no transitive dependency); when to intentionally denormalise
- `primary-foreign-keys` — drill: PK = unique + NOT NULL; FK = referential integrity; ON DELETE CASCADE vs SET NULL vs RESTRICT
- `indexes-basics` — drill: B-tree index, when to index (high-cardinality WHERE/JOIN columns), composite index column order matters, write overhead cost
- `acid-properties` — drill: all four properties in one sentence each; which property prevents dirty reads (Isolation)
- `transactions-basics` — drill: BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK, four anomalies (dirty/non-repeatable/phantom read + lost update), READ COMMITTED vs SERIALIZABLE
- `database-relationships` — drill: one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many via junction table; when to split into separate tables
- `comparisons` — drill: SQL vs NoSQL when to choose each, optimistic vs pessimistic locking concept
- `scenario-based` — drill: design e-commerce schema (users, products, orders, order_items), normalise a messy table, identify missing indexes

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- "What are ACID properties?" → Atomicity: transaction is all-or-nothing; Consistency: DB constraints are preserved; Isolation: concurrent transactions don't see each other's partial work; Durability: committed data survives failure
- "What is the difference between 2NF and 3NF?" → 2NF removes partial dependencies on composite PKs; 3NF removes transitive dependencies where a non-key column depends on another non-key column
- "What is an index and what are its trade-offs?" → B-tree structure that speeds reads on indexed columns; costs extra storage and slows writes (index must be updated on every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE)
- "What is the difference between optimistic and pessimistic locking?" → Optimistic: no lock, checks for conflict at commit time (version number); Pessimistic: locks row for exclusive access during the transaction
- "When would you choose MongoDB over PostgreSQL?" → Document model for flexible, nested, schema-less data; PostgreSQL for structured data with complex relationships and strong consistency

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"When I design a schema I start with normalisation — I aim for 3NF to eliminate redundancy and update anomalies. Every table has a primary key, and I use foreign keys to enforce referential integrity between tables. For performance I add indexes on columns used in WHERE and JOIN conditions, but I'm conscious that every index adds overhead to writes. For transactions I rely on ACID properties — particularly Isolation to ensure concurrent users don't see each other's partial work and Atomicity to ensure a multi-step operation either fully completes or fully rolls back."*
